Rava objects that the verse 'עַל שֵׁם אֲחֵיהֶם יִקָּרְאוּ' shows Ephraim and Menashe are only equated to tribes for inheritance, not for other matters.
Rava objects that the verse equating Ephraim and Menashe to Reuben and Simeon applies only to inheritance (נחלה), not to other matters like the count of tribes for the bull-offering.

items.text: Refutation of Rava: They are distinct in banners and princes
items.text_en: Refutation of Rava: They are distinct in banners and princes
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava by noting that Ephraim and Menashe were distinct in the banners (camps) and in the princes' offerings. The response is that these distinctions were only for honor, not for halakhic status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rava by noting that Ephraim and Menashe were distinct in the banners (דגלים).
The Gemara answers that their distinct banners were only for honor, not for halakhic status.
The Gemara further objects that Ephraim and Menashe had distinct princes (נשיאים).
The Gemara answers that the separate princes were also only for honor, citing a baraita that Solomon's dedication and Moses's princes' offerings were for honor.

items.text: Transition: What is the conclusion?
items.text_en: Transition: What is the conclusion?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the conclusion is regarding the matter of the tribes and the bull-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the conclusion is regarding the dispute between Abaye and Rava.

items.text: Baraita: Five sin-offerings that die; application to the community
items.text_en: Baraita: Five sin-offerings that die; application to the community
items.desc_en: A baraita from Rabbi Shimon lists five sin-offerings that must die, and notes that three do not apply to the community. For the remaining two, the Gemara infers from the explicit cases that they also apply only to an individual, not the community. The Gemara questions the logic of inferring from a possible case to an impossible one, and resolves that Rabbi Shimon learned this from a tradition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon lists five sin-offerings that must die, and notes that three of them (ולד חטאת, תמורת חטאת, and חטאת שמתו בעליה) cannot apply to the community.

The Gemara notes that for the remaining two cases (חטאת שנתכפרו בעליה and חטאת שעברה שנתה), the baraita does not explicitly state whether they apply to the community, and asks: could they also die in the community context?
The Gemara infers from the explicit cases (which apply only to an individual) to the implicit ones, concluding that all five sin-offerings apply only to an individual, not the community.

The Gemara objects: how can one infer from a possible case (an individual's sin-offering) to an impossible one (the community's sin-offering), since the community cannot have a female offering or a substitute?
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon learned this halacha (הלכה) from a tradition (גמיר) received at one place, not through logical inference.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter: 'We return to you, the court erred'
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter: 'We return to you, the court erred'
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter with the standard formula 'Hadran alach Horu Beit Din'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).

items.text: Mishnah: The anointed priest's liability for erroneous ruling
items.text_en: Mishnah: The anointed priest's liability for erroneous ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the anointed priest erroneously ruled for himself and then acted erroneously, he brings a bull. If he ruled erroneously but acted intentionally, or ruled intentionally but acted erroneously, he is exempt, because his ruling for himself is like the court's ruling for the community.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the anointed priest errs and acts inadvertently, he brings a bull; if he errs but acts intentionally or vice versa, he is exempt, as his self-ruling is like the court's ruling for the community.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the case of 'erred and acted erroneously'
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the case of 'erred and acted erroneously'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah states the obvious case of erring and acting erroneously. Abaye explains that it deals with a case where the priest forgot the reason for his ruling but acted based on his original ruling, lest one think he is considered intentional. The Mishnah teaches that he is still liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah states the obvious case of 'erred and acted erroneously' — it is self-evident.

Abaye explains that the case involves a priest who forgot the reason for his ruling but acted based on his original ruling, and the Mishnah teaches that he is still liable, lest one think he is considered intentional.

items.text: Source for the exemption of intentional ruling or action
items.text_en: Source for the exemption of intentional ruling or action
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the Mishnah's ruling that if the priest ruled intentionally or acted intentionally he is exempt. It cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'for the guilt of the people' that the anointed priest is like the community, and a logical inference is possible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that an intentional ruling followed by an inadvertent act exempts the priest, and begins to cite a baraita that equates the anointed priest to the community.
The baraita cites the verse 'for the guilt of the people' to establish that the anointed priest is like the community, and then notes that a logical inference is possible.

items.text: Deriving the anointed priest's liability from the community
items.text_en: Deriving the anointed priest's liability from the community
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares the anointed priest to the community (צבור) and to the prince (נשיא) to determine whether he requires both העלם דבר and שגגת מעשה. It concludes from the verse 'לאשמת העם' that he is like the community, requiring both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a comparison: just as the community (צבור) is derived from the category of an individual and requires both העלם דבר (unawareness of the prohibition) and שגגת מעשה (erroneous action), so too the anointed priest should require both.
An alternative comparison is raised: the anointed priest could be compared to the prince (נשיא), who brings a sacrifice for erroneous action alone without העלם דבר.

The Gemara resolves the comparison: the anointed priest is like the community because both bring a bull (פר) and do not bring an אשם תלוי (conditional guilt-offering), so he requires both העלם דבר and שגגת מעשה.

Another alternative comparison is raised: the anointed priest could be compared to the prince because both bring a female goat (שעירה) for idolatry and a definite guilt-offering (אשם ודאי), so he should require only erroneous action.
The Gemara concludes with a scriptural derivation: the verse 'לאשמת העם' (to the guilt of the people) equates the anointed priest to the community, so he requires both העלם דבר and שגגת מעשה.

items.text: Rejecting a possible inference about others' sin
items.text_en: Rejecting a possible inference about others' sin
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects a potential inference that the anointed priest would be liable when others act on his ruling, citing the verse 'על חטאתו אשר חטא' to show he brings only for his own sin, not for others'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possible inference: just as the community is liable when they follow the court's ruling, so too the anointed priest should be liable when others act on his ruling.
The Gemara rejects the inference by citing the verse 'על חטאתו אשר חטא' (for his sin which he sinned), showing that the anointed priest brings only for his own sin, not for the sins of others.

items.text: Source that the anointed priest does not bring a suspensive guilt-offering
items.text_en: Source that the anointed priest does not bring a suspensive guilt-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the anointed priest does not bring an אשם תלוי, and derives it from the verse 'וכפר עליו הכהן על שגגתו אשר שגג', requiring that his sin and unwitting act be equal, which is not the case for the anointed priest who is like the community.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that the anointed priest brings a bull and does not bring a suspensive guilt-offering, and the Gemara asks for the source of this ruling.

The Gemara derives from the verse 'וכפר עליו הכהן על שגגתו אשר שגג' that only one whose sin and unwitting act are equal brings a suspensive guilt-offering, excluding the anointed priest whose sin is like the community's.
The Gemara objects that the verse 'לאשמת העם' was not yet stated at that point, and resolves that the derivation is from the word 'אשם' as it is taken.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on atonement when ruling with the community
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on atonement when ruling with the community
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the anointed priest rules alone and acts alone, he atones alone; if he rules with the community and acts with them, he atones with them. The Gemara derives this from a comparison to the prince (נשיא), rejecting a counter-argument based on Yom Kippur atonement, and concludes with the verse 'על חטאתו אשר חטא'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: if the anointed priest rules alone and acts alone, he atones alone; if he rules with the community and acts with them, he atones with them, and the same applies to the court and to idolatry.
The Gemara asks: From where are these matters derived? It cites a baraita that raises the possibility that the anointed priest might bring a bull for himself even when he ruled with the community.
The baraita proposes a logical inference: just as a king (נשיא) who sins alone brings his offering alone and who sins with the community atones with them, so too the anointed priest.
The Gemara objects: the analogy to the king fails because the king atones with the community on Yom Kippur, whereas the anointed priest does not.

The Gemara resolves: since the anointed priest does not atone with the community on Yom Kippur, one might think he brings a bull for himself, but the verse 'על חטאתו אשר חטא' (for his sin that he sinned) teaches that if he sinned alone he brings alone, and if he sinned with the community he atones with them.

items.text: Clarifying the cases of ruling with the community
items.text_en: Clarifying the cases of ruling with the community
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's case: if the priest is an expert and they are not, he atones alone; if they are experts and he is not, his ruling is void and he does not atone alone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances? If the priest is a distinguished scholar and they are not, it is obvious that he atones alone, and each individual must bring a ewe or goat.
The Gemara asks: if the judges are distinguished scholars and he is not, why would he atone alone? His ruling is nothing at all.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of a case where the court and the priest rule on different prohibitions
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of a case where the court and the priest rule on different prohibitions
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa presents a case where both the court and the priest are experts. Abaye and Rava debate whether the court and priest are considered separate entities when they rule on different prohibitions. The Gemara then explores various scenarios, such as one ruling on forbidden fat and the other on idolatry, and raises a question about whether different types of forbidden fat are considered distinct prohibitions, concluding with a teiku (undecided).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa presents a case where both the court and the priest are experts (מופלים).
Abaye proposes that the court and priest are separate entities when they rule on different prohibitions, even if in different locations.
Rava objects that location is irrelevant; the key is that they rule on different prohibitions, making it a separate sin.
The Gemara clarifies that if the priest rules on forbidden fat and the court on idolatry, they are clearly separate because they differ in both reasoning and offerings.
The Gemara raises a question: if the priest rules on one type of forbidden fat and the court on another, are they considered separate prohibitions or one category?
The Gemara poses a further unresolved question: if the priest rules on forbidden fat and the court on blood, are they separate due to differing reasons or do we follow the similarity of offerings?

items.text: Derivation that the court must rule to partially nullify and partially uphold the law
items.text_en: Derivation that the court must rule to partially nullify and partially uphold the law
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the court is liable only when they rule to partially nullify and partially uphold the law. It cites a derivation from the word 'davar' (matter) in another chapter, indicating that the ruling must be on a matter, not the entire body of law. It then extends this to the anointed priest via the verse 'le'ashmat ha'am' and to idolatry through a gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) on 'me'einei'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the court is liable only when they rule to partially nullify and partially uphold the law.
The Gemara cites the derivation from the word 'דבר' (matter) in another chapter, indicating that the ruling must be on a matter, not the entire body of law.

sub.text: Gemara's extension to the anointed priest
sub.text_en: Gemara's extension to the anointed priest
sub.desc_en: The Gemara extends the same principle to the anointed priest via the verse 'לאשמת העם' (for the guilt of the people), equating the priest with the community.

sub.text: Gemara's extension to idolatry via gezerah shavah
sub.text_en: Gemara's extension to idolatry via gezerah shavah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara extends the principle to idolatry through a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on 'מעיני', showing that the same rule of 'דבר' applies.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on liability requiring concealment of the matter with an erroneous action
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on liability requiring concealment of the matter with an erroneous action
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the court and the anointed priest are liable only for a ruling that involves concealment of the matter (he'elem davar) combined with an erroneous action (shigegat ha'ma'aseh). The Gemara derives this from the verse 'yishgu vene'elam davar' for the court, and for the priest from 'le'ashmat ha'am'. For idolatry, a gezerah shavah on 'me'einei' teaches the same requirement.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the court and the anointed priest are liable only for a ruling involving concealment of the matter (העלם דבר) combined with an erroneous action (שגגת המעשה).
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive this requirement for the court?

A baraita is cited: The verse 'יִשְׁגּוּ' might imply liability for mere erroneous action, but the continuation 'וְנֶעֱלַם דָּבָר' teaches that liability requires both concealment of the matter and an erroneous action.
The Gemara derives the same requirement for the anointed priest from the verse 'לְאַשְׁמַת הָעָם', equating the priest to the community.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive this requirement for idolatry?

A baraita is cited: Since idolatry is treated separately, one might think liability applies to mere erroneous action; a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on 'מֵעֵינֵי' teaches that here too liability requires concealment of the matter with an erroneous action.

items.text: Debate about the anointed priest's liability for idolatry and the source for his offering
items.text_en: Debate about the anointed priest's liability for idolatry and the source for his offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not mention the anointed priest in the context of idolatry, and identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi's opinion. A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi holds the priest is liable for an erroneous action, while the Sages require concealment of the matter. Both agree the priest brings a female goat and does not bring a suspensive guilt-offering. The Gemara explains Rabbi's derivation from the verse 'vechipper ha'kohen al hanefesh hashogeges' and the Sages' counter-argument. Finally, it derives that all individuals (commoner, prince, priest) are included in 'nefesh achat' for the female goat offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not mention the anointed priest in the context of idolatry, and identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi's opinion.

A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi holds the priest is liable for an erroneous action, while the Sages require concealment of the matter; both agree the priest brings a female goat and does not bring a suspensive guilt-offering.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah does not mention the priest's liability for intentional idolatry, and resolves that the Mishnah teaches one case and the same applies to the other.

The Gemara explains Rabbi's derivation from the verse 'וְכִפֶּר הַכֹּהֵן עַל הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַשֹּׁגֶגֶת בְּחֶטְאָה בִשְׁגָגָה' (and the priest shall atone for the soul that errs in sin unintentionally), interpreting 'the soul' as the anointed priest and 'that errs' as the prince, and Rabbi holds that the sin must be unintentional.
The Sages counter that the verse refers to one whose sin-offering is for an unintentional act, excluding the anointed priest whose sin-offering is for concealment of the matter.
The Gemara derives that all individuals (commoner, prince, priest) are included in 'נֶפֶשׁ אַחַת' (one soul) for the female goat offering.

items.text: Derivation that the anointed priest does not bring a provisional guilt offering
items.text_en: Derivation that the anointed priest does not bring a provisional guilt offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'and the priest shall make atonement for him for his error which he erred' that only one whose entire sin is in error brings an asham talui, excluding the anointed priest whose sin involves העלם דבר. Rabbi holds that the word 'אשר' implies 'all his sin', while the Rabbis hold that the phrase 'his sin is in error' suffices to exclude the anointed priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that all agree the anointed priest does not bring an אשם תלוי (provisional guilt-offering), and asks for the source, citing the verse 'וכפר עליו הכהן על שגגתו אשר שגג' (and the priest shall atone for him for his error which he erred).
The Gemara questions Rabbi's interpretation: is the word 'כל' (all) actually written in the verse?

The Gemara answers that the extra word 'אשר' (which) implies 'all his sin', and therefore the anointed priest is excluded because his sin involves העלם דבר (absence of awareness of the matter) rather than pure error.

The Rabbis hold that the phrase 'whose sin is in error' suffices to exclude the anointed priest, since his sin is not in error but in העלם דבר (absence of awareness of the matter) together with unwitting action.

items.text: Mishnah: Liability only for matters with karet and sin offering
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability only for matters with karet and sin offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a court and the anointed priest are liable only if they rule on a matter whose intentional violation is karet and unintentional violation is a sin offering, and similarly for idolatry.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a court and the anointed priest are liable only if they rule on a matter whose intentional violation is karet and unintentional violation is a sin offering, and similarly for idolatry.

items.text: Derivation for court, anointed priest, leader, and individual regarding non-idolatry
items.text_en: Derivation for court, anointed priest, leader, and individual regarding non-idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the Mishnah's rule. Rabbi uses a גזירה שוה from 'עליה' to derive that the court is liable only for matters with karet and sin offering. The anointed priest is derived from 'לאשמת העם', the leader from a גזירה שוה of 'מצות' with the court, and the individual from the verse 'ואם נפש' learning from the higher category.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the Mishnah's rule that the court is liable only for matters with karet and sin offering.
Rabbi cites a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) from 'עליה' to derive that the court is liable only for matters with karet and sin offering.
The Gemara derives the anointed priest from the verse 'לאשמת העם', equating him with the community.
The Gemara derives the leader from a גזירה שוה of 'מצות' with the court, applying the same standard.
The Gemara derives the individual from the verse 'ואם נפש', learning the lower category from the higher one.

items.text: Derivation for idolatry: court and individuals
items.text_en: Derivation for idolatry: court and individuals
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that for idolatry, the court is liable only for matters with karet and sin offering via a גזירה שוה from 'מעיני'. For the individual, leader, and anointed priest, the verse 'ואם נפש אחת' includes them all, learning from the higher category.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for idolatry (עבודה זרה), what is the source that the court is liable only for matters with karet and sin offering, and could one think they are liable even for lesser matters?
The baraita applies a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) from 'מעיני' to derive that for idolatry, the court is liable only for matters with karet and sin offering.

The Gemara resolves that for the individual, leader, and anointed priest, the verse 'ואם נפש אחת' includes them all, learning from the higher category (the court) that they too are liable only for matters with karet and sin offering.

items.text: Alternative derivation for the Rabbis who do not use the גזירה שוה
items.text_en: Alternative derivation for the Rabbis who do not use the גזירה שוה
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the Rabbis who use 'עליה' for forbidden relations and rival wives, what is their source? Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi taught his son that all Torah is equated to idolatry via the verse 'תורה אחת', so that just as idolatry requires karet and sin offering, so do all commandments. This provides the source for the individual, leader, and anointed priest; the court is derived from the lower category.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the Rabbis who use the word 'עליה' for forbidden relations and rival wives, what is their source for the rule that liability applies only to a matter whose intentional violation is karet and whose unintentional violation is a sin offering?

The Gemara answers that they derive it from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's teaching to his son, who equated all Torah to idolatry via the verse 'תורה אחת', so that just as idolatry requires karet and a sin offering, so do all commandments.

The Gemara concludes that this source provides the rule for the individual, leader, and anointed priest; the court is derived from the lower category (תחתון) learning from the higher category (עליון).

items.text: Rabbi's use of the verse and objection by Rav Chilkiah
items.text_en: Rabbi's use of the verse and objection by Rav Chilkiah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi uses the verse 'תורה אחת' for a different teaching: that even though the Torah distinguishes between the community (execution by sword, property lost) and individuals (stoning, property saved), one might think their offerings differ, but the verse teaches they are the same. Rav Chilkiah objects: if the verse had not distinguished, we would have thought they differ; what offering would we have brought? The Gemara explores various possibilities and concludes that the verse teaches that no alternative offering is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi uses the verse 'תורה אחת' to teach that despite the Torah's distinction between the community (execution by sword, property lost) and individuals (stoning, property saved), their offerings are the same.
Rav Chilkiah objects: if the verse had distinguished, we would have thought the offerings differ; what alternative offering would we have brought?
The Gemara explores various possible alternative offerings (bull, bull for burnt-offering and goat for sin-offering, goat, she-goat) and notes that each would duplicate an existing offering category.

The Gemara concludes that the verse teaches that no alternative offering is needed, countering the possible thought that individuals would bring the opposite type (bull for sin-offering, goat for burnt-offering) or that they would have no remedy.

items.text: Proof that the verses refer to idolatry
items.text_en: Proof that the verses refer to idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since everyone agrees these verses are written regarding idolatry, what indicates this? Rava (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) says the verse 'וכי תשגו ולא תעשו את כל המצות האלה' refers to a commandment equivalent to all commandments, which is idolatry. The school of Rabbi taught that the verse 'אשר דבר ה' אל משה' and 'אשר צוה ה' אליכם ביד משה' refers to a commandment spoken by God and commanded through Moses, which is idolatry, as Rabbi Yishmael taught that 'אנכי' and 'לא יהיה לך' were heard from the Almighty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since everyone agrees these verses are written regarding idolatry, what indicates this?
Rava (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) answers that the verse 'וכי תשגו ולא תעשו את כל המצות האלה' refers to a commandment equivalent to all commandments, which is idolatry.
The school of Rabbi taught that the verse 'אשר דבר ה' אל משה' and 'אשר צוה ה' אליכם ביד משה' refers to a commandment spoken by God and commanded through Moses, which is idolatry.
Rabbi Yishmael taught that 'אנכי' and 'לא יהיה לך' were heard from the Almighty, supporting that idolatry is the commandment spoken directly by God.

items.text: Opening question on the first commandment
items.text_en: Opening question on the first commandment
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which commandment was given first, suggesting it is idolatry, but then raises a contradiction from Mar that ten commandments were given at Marah. It resolves by saying the matter is as we originally explained.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which commandment was given first, and answers that it is idolatry.
The Gemara objects that Mar said ten commandments were given at Marah, contradicting the claim that idolatry was first.
The Gemara resolves that the matter is as originally explained, presumably reconciling the two sources.

items.text: Mishnah: Liability for Temple and Niddah commandments
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for Temple and Niddah commandments
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is not liable for a fixed sin-offering or a suspensive guilt-offering for positive or negative commandments related to the Temple, but one is liable for those related to niddah. It specifies the positive commandment as separating from the niddah and the negative as not coming upon her.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is not liable for a fixed sin-offering or a suspensive guilt-offering for positive or negative commandments related to the Temple.
The Mishnah contrasts that one is liable for positive and negative commandments related to niddah, specifying the positive as separating from the niddah and the negative as not coming upon her.

items.text: Gemara's derivation for community and individual liability
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation for community and individual liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the community is not liable for a general offering and the individual not for a suspensive guilt-offering. Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi derives from a verbal analogy between 've'ashem' in the individual's fixed sin-offering and 've'ashemu' in the community, and extends it to the suspensive guilt-offering. An objection is raised about the sliding-scale offering, but it is rejected because the analogy is from 'ashem' to 'ashemu', not from 'ashem' to 'ye'sham'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the community is not liable for a general offering and the individual not for a suspensive guilt-offering.

Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi derives from a verbal analogy between 'וְאָשֵׁם' (ve'ashem) in the individual's fixed sin-offering and 'וְאָשֵׁמוּ' (ve'ashemu) in the community, concluding that the community is liable only for a fixed sin-offering.
Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi extends the analogy to the suspensive guilt-offering (אשם תלוי), showing it only comes for a doubt of a fixed sin-offering.
An objection is raised: if so, the sliding-scale offering (קרבן עולה ויורד) should also be excluded, since the verse uses 'יֶאְשַׁם' (ye'sham).
The Gemara rejects the objection: the analogy is drawn from 'אָשֵׁם' (ashem) to 'אָשֵׁמוּ' (ashemu), not from 'אָשֵׁם' to 'יֶאְשַׁם' (ye'sham), so the sliding-scale offering is not included.

items.text: Challenge to the derivation from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Challenge to the derivation from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the verbal analogy, noting that the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that 'return' and 'come' are the same, and suggests learning from the 'ashem' in the context of Temple and its sancta impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the derivation by noting that the school of Rabbi Yishmael treats 'return' and 'come' as equivalent, and suggests learning from the 'וְאָשֵׁם' in the context of טומאת מקדש וקדשיו (impurity of the Temple and its sancta).

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's refined derivations
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's refined derivations
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa proposes a derivation using 've'ashem' and 'mitzvot Hashem', but Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects by suggesting a different phrase. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak then offers a more precise derivation using 've'ashem' and 'mitzvot Hashem asher lo te'asenah', excluding other cases like hearing the voice and utterance of the lips.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa proposes a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between the terms 'וְאָשֵׁם' (and he shall be guilty) and 'מִצְוֹת ה׳' (commandments of the Lord) in the context of the individual's guilt-offering and the community's guilt, to derive the law.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects that one could equally derive a verbal analogy using the phrase 'וְאָשֵׁם' and 'נְשִׂיאַת עָוֹן' (bearing iniquity), which would lead to a different conclusion.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's refined derivation
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's refined derivation
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the objection by offering a more precise verbal analogy using the full phrase 'וְאָשֵׁם' and 'מִצְוֹת ה׳ אֲשֶׁר לֹא תֵעָשֶׂינָה' (commandments of the Lord that are not to be done), which excludes the cases of hearing the voice, utterance of the lips, and impurity of the Temple and its sanctified items, since those do not contain this exact phrase.

items.text: Mishnah: The king's liability for certain offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: The king's liability for certain offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is not liable for hearing the voice, utterance of the lips, or Temple impurity, and the king is similar according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili. Rabbi Akiva says the king is liable for all except hearing the voice, because the king does not judge nor is judged, and does not testify nor is testified about.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is not liable for hearing the voice, utterance of the lips, or Temple impurity, and the king is similar according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
Rabbi Akiva says the king is liable for all except hearing the voice, because the king does not judge nor is judged, and does not testify nor is testified about.

items.text: Gemara: Ulla's explanation of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara: Ulla's explanation of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's reasoning
items.desc_en: Ulla explains Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's reasoning from the verse 'when he shall be guilty in one of these', implying that one who is liable for one is liable for all. The Gemara objects that it could mean liable for one even if not for all, so it cites a baraita where Rabbi Yirmeya derives the same point from another source.

sub.desc_en: Ulla asks what is Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's reasoning, and explains that the verse 'when he shall be guilty in one of these' implies that one who is liable for one is liable for all.
The Gemara objects that the verse could mean liable for one even if not for all.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's reasoning actually comes from a baraita where Rabbi Yirmeya derives the same point from another source.

items.text: Exemption of Nasi and Mashiach from poverty-based offerings
items.text_en: Exemption of Nasi and Mashiach from poverty-based offerings
items.desc_en: The gemara explains that the verses 'lo tagi'a yado' and 'lo tasig yado' refer to one who experiences poverty and wealth, excluding the nasi and mashiach who do not come to poverty. The nasi is exempt because the verse says 'v'asah achat mikol mitzvot Hashem Elohav' implying he has only God above him, and the mashiach because he is 'gadol me'echav' in beauty, strength, wisdom, and wealth. Aherim add that if he lacks wealth, we make him great from his brothers.

sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that the verses 'לֹא תַגִּיעַ יָדוֹ' and 'לֹא תַשִּׂיג יָדוֹ' refer to one who experiences poverty and wealth, excluding the nasi and mashiach who do not come to poverty.
The gemara cites the verse 'וְעָשָׂה אַחַת מִכָּל מִצְוֹת ה׳ אֱלֹהָיו' to show the nasi has only God above him, exempting him from poverty.
The gemara cites the verse 'וְהַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדוֹל מֵאֶחָיו' to show the mashiach is greater than his brothers in beauty, strength, wisdom, and wealth.
Aherim add that if the mashiach lacks wealth, we make him great from his brothers, citing the verse 'וְהַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדוֹל מֵאֶחָיו אֲשֶׁר יוּצַק עַל רֹאשׁוֹ'.

items.text: Ravina's inquiry about a leprous nasi
items.text_en: Ravina's inquiry about a leprous nasi
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak whether a nasi who becomes a leper is dismissed from office or exempt from offerings. Rav Nachman responds with a cryptic question: 'Is it yours or of the shearer?'

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak whether a nasi who becomes a leper is dismissed from office or exempt from offerings.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's cryptic response
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's cryptic response
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak responds with a cryptic question: 'Is it yours or of the shearer?'

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's view and its derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's view and its derivation
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Akiva says the mashiach is exempt from all variable offerings. Rava explains the reason: the verse 'zeh korban Aharon uvanav' indicates that only this offering (the tenth of an ephah) is obligatory for him, and no other. The gemara then questions whether the exemption applies only to poverty (the tenth of an ephah) but not to wealth-based offerings, but concludes that the verse 'v'chiper alav hakohen al chatato asher chata me'achat me'eleh' implies that one who is atoned through one is atoned through all, and one who is not atoned through one is not atoned through all.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Akiva's ruling that the mashiach (anointed high priest) is exempt from all variable sin-offerings.

Rava explains Rabbi Akiva's reasoning: the verse 'זֶה קׇרְבַּן אַהֲרֹן וּבָנָיו' (this is the offering of Aaron and his sons) teaches that only the tenth of an ephah is obligatory for the high priest, and no other offering is obligatory for him.

The gemara objects: perhaps the verse only exempts the mashiach from the offering of poverty (עֲשִׂירִית הָאֵיפָה, the tenth of an ephah), but not from offerings based on wealth or poverty (עֲנִיּוּת וַעֲשִׁירוּת).

The gemara rejects the objection: the verse 'וְכִפֶּר עָלָיו הַכֹּהֵן עַל חַטָּאתוֹ אֲשֶׁר חָטָא מֵאַחַת מֵאֵלֶּה' (and the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin which he sinned from one of these) implies that one who is atoned through one offering is atoned through all, and one who is not atoned through one is not atoned through all, thus the mashiach's exemption from the tenth of an ephah extends to all variable offerings.

items.text: Challenge from the nasi's liability for sh'maat kol
items.text_en: Challenge from the nasi's liability for sh'maat kol
items.desc_en: The gemara challenges the previous reasoning by noting that the verse 'v'haya ki ye'sham l'achat me'eleh' would similarly imply that one liable for one is liable for all, yet we have a mishna where Rabbi Akiva says the nasi is liable except for sh'maat kol, contradicting that implication.

sub.desc_en: The gemara challenges that the verse 'וְהָיָה כִּי יֶאְשַׁם לְאַחַת מֵאֵלֶּה' would imply universal liability for all sins if liable for one, yet the mishna (Rabbi Akiva) rules the nasi is liable except for שמיעת קול (the law of hearing a public adjuration), creating a contradiction.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava both state that 'me'achat' implies inclusion, while 'l'achat' does not. They explain that the word 'me'achat' is written at the end regarding the tenth of an ephah to teach that whoever is liable for the tenth of an ephah is liable for all, because if one could be liable for one without being liable for all, the verse would have written 'me'achat me'eleh' in the context of poverty or wealth.

sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rava state that the word 'מאחת' (from one) implies inclusion of all, while 'לאחת' (to one) does not.
The Gemara asks why specifically the word 'מאחת' implies inclusion.

The Gemara explains that the Torah wrote 'מאחת' at the end regarding the tenth of an ephah to teach that whoever is liable for that offering is liable for all, because if one could be liable for one without all, the verse would have written 'מאחת מאלה' in the context of poverty or wealth.

items.text: Mishna: Offerings for various sins
items.text_en: Mishna: Offerings for various sins
items.desc_en: The mishna lists the offerings brought for sins that incur karet for intentional violation and a chatat for unintentional: an individual brings a kisbah or se'irah, a nasi a sa'ir, and the mashiach and court bring a par. For idolatry, the individual, nasi, and mashiach bring a se'irah, and the court a par and sa'ir. For asham talui, the individual and nasi are liable, while mashiach and court are exempt. For asham vadai, the individual, nasi, and mashiach are liable, but the court is exempt. For sh'maat kol, bitui sfatayim, and tum'at mikdash v'kadashav, the court is exempt, and the individual, nasi, and mashiach are liable, except that the anointed high priest is not liable for tum'at mikdash v'kadashav according to Rabbi Shimon. They bring a korban oleh v'yored. Rabbi Eliezer says the nasi brings a sa'ir.

sub.desc_en: The mishna opens by listing the offerings for sins incurring karet for intentional violation and a chatat for unintentional: an individual brings a kisbah or se'irah, a nasi a sa'ir, and the mashiach and court bring a par; for idolatry, the individual, nasi, and mashiach bring a se'irah, and the court a par and sa'ir.

The mishna states that for asham talui, the individual and nasi are liable, while mashiach and court are exempt; for asham vadai, the individual, nasi, and mashiach are liable, but the court is exempt.

The mishna concludes that for sh'maat kol, bitui sfatayim, and tum'at mikdash v'kadashav, the court is exempt, and the individual, nasi, and mashiach are liable, except that the anointed high priest is not liable for tum'at mikdash v'kadashav according to Rabbi Shimon; they bring a korban oleh v'yored, and Rabbi Eliezer says the nasi brings a sa'ir.

items.text: Gemara on Rabbi Shimon's rule and a contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara on Rabbi Shimon's rule and a contradiction
items.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Shimon's rule: for asham talui, the nasi is like an individual, and mashiach and court are exempt; for asham vadai, nasi and mashiach are like individuals, and court is exempt; for sh'maat kol, bitui sfatayim, and tum'at mikdash v'kadashav, court is exempt, nasi and mashiach are liable, except that the nasi is not liable for sh'maat kol and the mashiach not for tum'at mikdash v'kadashav; for oleh v'yored, the nasi is like an individual, and mashiach and court are exempt. The gemara then points out a contradiction: the baraita says the mashiach is exempt from tum'at mikdash v'kadashav but implies he is liable for sh'maat kol and bitui sfatayim, yet the end says mashiach and court are exempt from all oleh v'yored, implying the mashiach is exempt from all of them.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Shimon's general rule: for cases where an individual brings an asham talui, the nasi is like him, while mashiach and court are exempt; for asham vadai, nasi and mashiach are like the individual, and court is exempt.

The baraita continues: for sh'maat kol, bitui sfatayim, and tum'at mikdash v'kadashav, court is exempt, nasi and mashiach are liable, except that the nasi is not liable for sh'maat kol and the mashiach not for tum'at mikdash v'kadashav; for oleh v'yored, the nasi is like an individual, and mashiach and court are exempt.

The gemara points out a contradiction: the baraita says the mashiach is exempt from tum'at mikdash v'kadashav but implies he is liable for sh'maat kol and bitui sfatayim, yet the end says mashiach and court are exempt from all oleh v'yored, implying the mashiach is exempt from all of them.

items.text: Resolution of contradiction between baraitot
items.text_en: Resolution of contradiction between baraitot
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua resolves an apparent contradiction between two baraitot by distinguishing between 'poverty' (דלות) and 'extreme poverty' (דלי דלות). He further explains that Rabbi Shimon agrees with Rabbi Akiva in one case and disagrees in another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes an apparent contradiction between two baraitot.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between 'poverty' (דלות) and 'extreme poverty' (דלי דלות), and explains Rabbi Shimon's partial agreement with Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Derivation of Rabbi Shimon's exemption for High Priest
items.text_en: Derivation of Rabbi Shimon's exemption for High Priest
items.desc_en: Chizkiya explains Rabbi Shimon's reason for exempting the High Priest from a sliding-scale offering: the verse 'and that soul shall be cut off from the midst of the congregation' implies one whose offering is equal to the congregation. The Gemara challenges this with the prince and priests, and Rava refines the derivation to one whose sin-offering is equal to individuals, i.e., the congregation.

sub.desc_en: Chizkiya explains Rabbi Shimon's reason for exempting the High Priest: the verse 'and that soul shall be cut off from the midst of the congregation' implies one whose offering is equal to the congregation, excluding the High Priest whose offering differs.
The Gemara objects that the prince also has an unequal offering, and the Gemara answers that the prince is equal in the atonement of Yom Kippur.
The Gemara objects that priests also are unequal in Yom Kippur atonement, and answers that priests are equal in other commandments of the entire year.

sub.text: Gemara's objection about the High Priest
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection about the High Priest
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the High Priest is also equal in other commandments, so Rava refines the derivation: the verse refers to one whose sin-offering is equal to individuals, i.e., the congregation.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan limits Rabbi Eliezer's opinion
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan limits Rabbi Eliezer's opinion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Eliezer only said that a prince brings a goat for impurity of the Temple and its sacred foods, because the Torah stated 'karet' for that sin as for a fixed sin.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan limits Rabbi Eliezer's opinion to cases of impurity of the Temple and its sacred foods, because the Torah stated 'karet' for that sin as for a fixed sin.

items.text: Rav Papa supports Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation
items.text_en: Rav Papa supports Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Papa argues that it is logical that Rabbi Eliezer only refers to impurity of the Temple, because if he meant all sins, the Mishnah should also mention the anointed priest bringing a bull for hearing a voice and utterance of lips. Since it does not, it implies the anointed priest is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa argues that Rabbi Eliezer's statement must refer only to impurity of the Temple and its sacred foods, because if it applied to all sins, the Mishnah would also mention the anointed priest bringing a bull for hearing a voice and utterance of lips, which it does not, implying the anointed priest is exempt.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Papa and response
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Papa and response
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Natan challenges Rav Papa: perhaps Rabbi Eliezer refers to all sins, and regarding the anointed priest he holds like Rabbi Akiva who exempts him from all. Rav Papa responds that Rabbi Akiva does not exempt him from the bull, and no further discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Natan challenges Rav Papa: perhaps Rabbi Eliezer refers to all sins, and regarding the anointed priest he holds like Rabbi Akiva who exempts him from all.
Rav Papa responds that Rabbi Akiva does not exempt the anointed priest from the bull, and no further discussion.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on Rabbi Eliezer's concession and a contradiction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on Rabbi Eliezer's concession and a contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Eliezer concedes that a prince does not bring a provisional guilt-offering. A tanna taught before Rav Sheshet that a provisional guilt-offering comes for impurity of the Temple, but Rav Sheshet identifies this as Rabbi Eliezer's view, creating a contradiction with Rabbi Yochanan's statement.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Eliezer concedes that a prince does not bring a provisional guilt-offering.
A Tanna taught before Rav Sheshet that a provisional guilt-offering comes for impurity of the Temple and its sacred items.
Rav Sheshet identifies the Tanna's statement as Rabbi Eliezer's view, who says that since the verse states 'karet' like a fixed sin, the prince brings a goat for it.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan said Rabbi Eliezer concedes that a prince does not bring a provisional guilt-offering, creating a contradiction.
The Gemara declares the contradiction unresolved.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of anointed priest and prince who sinned after or before removal from office
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of anointed priest and prince who sinned after or before removal from office
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if an anointed priest or prince sinned and then left office, they bring their original offering. If they left office and then sinned, the anointed priest brings a bull, but the prince brings a commoner's offering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the law: an anointed priest or prince who sinned and then left office brings their original offering; if they left office and then sinned, the priest brings a bull but the prince brings a commoner's offering.

items.text: Gemara's opening question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's opening question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins its analysis of the Mishnah with a question: 'Now, can it be said: He passed from his anointment...'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a question: 'Now, can it be said: He passed from his anointment...'

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's redundancy
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's redundancy
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that if the High Priest sinned and then was removed from office, he brings a bull; it seems obvious. It explains that the Mishnah teaches this because it taught a similar case regarding the prince, and therefore it also taught it regarding the High Priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state the obvious case of a High Priest who sinned after being removed, and explains it is parallel to the prince's case.

items.text: Source for the High Priest bringing a sacrifice after removal
items.text_en: Source for the High Priest bringing a sacrifice after removal
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'וְהִקְרִיב עַל חַטָּאתוֹ' that the High Priest brings his sin-offering even after he has passed from his office. This is despite a logical argument that would suggest otherwise, comparing the prince and the High Priest.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'וְהִקְרִיב עַל חַטָּאתוֹ' that the High Priest brings his sin-offering even after he has passed from office, countering a possible קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from the prince.
The baraita cites the verse 'וְהִקְרִיב עַל חַטָּאתוֹ' to teach that the High Priest brings his sin-offering even after he has passed from office.
The baraita raises a logical argument (קל וחומר) that would suggest the High Priest should not bring a sacrifice after removal, comparing him to the prince.
The baraita resolves the argument by citing the verse, teaching that the High Priest brings his sin-offering after removal despite the logical objection.

items.text: Rejection of a kal vachomer for the prince
items.text_en: Rejection of a kal vachomer for the prince
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers a kal vachomer that the prince should also bring a sacrifice after removal, but the verse 'אֲשֶׁר נָשִׂיא יֶחֱטָא' teaches that he brings only while he is a prince, not when he is a commoner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the prince should also bring his sin-offering after removal via a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from the High Priest, but the verse 'אֲשֶׁר נָשִׂיא יֶחֱטָא' limits it to when he is still prince.
The Gemara rejects the kal vachomer by citing the verse 'אֲשֶׁר נָשִׂיא יֶחֱטָא' (when a prince sins), which implies he brings only while he is a prince, not when he is a commoner.

items.text: Mishnah: Sins before appointment and definition of prince
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sins before appointment and definition of prince
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a court sinned before being appointed, they are like commoners. Rabbi Shimon distinguishes based on when the sin became known. It then defines a prince as a king, based on the verse that he has no one above him except God.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a court sinned before being appointed and then were appointed, they are like commoners (הדיוטות) and exempt from the special court offering.
Rabbi Shimon distinguishes: if the sin became known before appointment, they are liable; if after appointment, they are exempt.
The Mishnah defines 'prince' (נשיא) as a king, based on the verse that he has no one above him except God.

items.text: Gemara: Source for excluding prior sins for the High Priest
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for excluding prior sins for the High Priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from 'אִם הַכֹּהֵן הַמָּשִׁיחַ יֶחֱטָא' that the High Priest does not bring a sacrifice for sins committed before his appointment. It presents a logical argument and a counter-argument, concluding with the verse that he brings only when he is the anointed priest.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from 'אִם הַכֹּהֵן הַמָּשִׁיחַ יֶחֱטָא' that the High Priest does not bring a sin-offering for sins committed before his appointment, rejecting a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from the prince.
The baraita cites the verse 'אִם הַכֹּהֵן הַמָּשִׁיחַ יֶחֱטָא' to exclude sins committed before his anointment.
The Gemara raises a logical argument (קל וחומר) from the prince (נשיא) to the High Priest, suggesting that the High Priest should also be exempt from bringing a sacrifice for prior sins.

The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that the prince does not bring a sacrifice for sins committed after his tenure, whereas the High Priest does, and concludes from the verse that the High Priest brings only when he is anointed.

items.text: Source for excluding prior sins for the prince
items.text_en: Source for excluding prior sins for the prince
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a similar baraita for the prince, deriving from 'אֲשֶׁר נָשִׂיא יֶחֱטָא' that he does not bring for prior sins. It presents a kal vachomer and a counter-argument, concluding that he brings only when he is a prince.

sub.desc_en: A baraita similarly derives from 'אֲשֶׁר נָשִׂיא יֶחֱטָא' that the prince does not bring a sin-offering for sins committed before his appointment, rejecting a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from the High Priest.
The gemara raises a kal vachomer: if the anointed priest does not bring for prior sins, surely the prince should not bring either.
The gemara rejects the kal vachomer by noting the priest's unique leniency (he does not bring for an erroneous action), and concludes from the verse that the prince brings only when he is a prince.

items.text: Discussion of 'גזרה' and the verse 'אם'
items.text_en: Discussion of 'גזרה' and the verse 'אם'
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a baraita that considers whether the verse 'אֲשֶׁר נָשִׂיא יֶחֱטָא' might imply a decree (גזרה) that he must sin, but the verse 'אִם' teaches that it is conditional. It then digresses to a discussion of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon regarding leprosy as a good tiding, and the derivation that leprosy is only from speech, with alternative explanations by Rava and Rav Papa.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by considering whether the verse 'אֲשֶׁר נָשִׂיא יֶחֱטָא' implies a decree (גזרה) that the king must sin, and resolves it by comparing to the verse 'אִם הַכֹּהֵן הַמָּשִׁיחַ יֶחֱטָא', which teaches that it is conditional.
The Gemara questions the baraita's premise: from where would the notion of a decree (גזרה) even arise?

The Gemara answers that a parallel exists: just as Rabbi Yehuda interprets the verse about leprosy in houses as a good tiding (בשורה), one might think the king's sin is decreed; but the verse 'אִם' teaches it is conditional.
The Gemara objects: according to Rabbi Shimon, do leprosy lesions caused by coercion (אונסין) not impart impurity? A baraita is cited to show that leprosy only comes from speech, not from coercion.
Rava and Rav Papa offer alternative explanations: Rava says the verse excludes leprosy caused by spirits (רוחות), and Rav Papa says it excludes leprosy caused by sorcery (כשפים).

items.text: Exclusion of a leprous prince
items.text_en: Exclusion of a leprous prince
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that excludes a sick person from the law of the prince, and Rav Avdimi bar Chama explains that it refers to a prince who became a leper, as leprosy removes him from his office, citing the verse about King Uzziah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita that excludes a sick prince, and Rav Avdimi bar Chama explains it refers to a leprous prince, citing the verse about King Uzziah.

Rav Avdimi bar Chama explains that the baraita refers to a prince who became a leper, as leprosy removes him from his office, citing the verse about King Uzziah who was stricken with leprosy and lived in a separate house, implying he was previously a servant.

items.text: Story of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Story of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story about Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua traveling on a ship, where Rabbi Yehoshua's foresight about a star that misleads sailors leads to a discussion about his students who are in need. Rabban Gamliel decides to appoint them to positions of authority, but they initially refuse.

sub.desc_en: A story about Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua at sea, where Rabbi Yehoshua's wisdom leads Rabban Gamliel to appoint Rabbi Elazar Chasma and Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgada to leadership.
Rabban Gamliel asks Rabbi Yehoshua if he knew they would be delayed, implying he brought extra flour deliberately.
Rabbi Yehoshua explains that a star that misleads sailors rises every seventy years, and he anticipated it might cause their delay.
Rabban Gamliel expresses astonishment that Rabbi Yehoshua, with such knowledge, would risk traveling by sea.
Rabbi Yehoshua redirects Rabban Gamliel's amazement to his two students, Rabbi Elazar Chasma and Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgada, who are brilliant but destitute.
Rabban Gamliel resolves to appoint these students to positions of leadership.
Upon arriving on land, Rabban Gamliel summons the students; they initially refuse but eventually come, and he asks if they think he is offering them mere authority.

items.text: The meaning of 'אשר' in the nasi's sin-offering
items.text_en: The meaning of 'אשר' in the nasi's sin-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a baraita where Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai interprets 'אשרי' as 'fortunate' for the generation whose nasi brings a sin-offering. Rava objects, citing the same word used for Jeroboam, and concludes that the verse uses a different expression.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai interpreting 'אשר' in the nasi's sin-offering as 'אשרי' (fortunate) for the generation whose nasi brings a sin-offering.
Rava objects that the same word 'אשר' is used for Jeroboam, who was wicked, so it cannot imply fortune.
The Gemara resolves that the case of the nasi is different because the verse uses a different expression (אשרי vs. אשר).

items.text: The righteous receiving the reward of the wicked in this world
items.text_en: The righteous receiving the reward of the wicked in this world
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda interprets a verse to mean that the righteous receive the reward of the wicked in this world, and vice versa. Rava objects, questioning why the righteous would not want both worlds, and reinterprets the verse to mean that the righteous receive the reward of the wicked of this world in this world.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda interprets the verse from Ecclesiastes to mean that the righteous receive in this world the reward meant for the wicked in the World-to-Come, and the wicked receive in this world the reward meant for the righteous in the World-to-Come.
Rava objects to Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's interpretation, questioning why the righteous would not want to enjoy both worlds.
Rava offers his own reinterpretation: the righteous receive in this world the reward of the wicked of this world, and the wicked receive in this world the suffering of the righteous of this world.

items.text: Rava's application of the verse to his students
items.text_en: Rava's application of the verse to his students
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua come before Rava and tell him they have studied and acquired a small piece of land. Rava applies the verse about the righteous receiving the reward of the wicked in this world to them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua come before Rava, who asks if they have mastered certain tractates and acquired wealth; they confirm both, mentioning they bought a small parcel of land.
Rava applies the verse about the righteous receiving the reward of the wicked in this world to them, declaring them happy.

items.text: The parable of the two paths and the story of Lot
items.text_en: The parable of the two paths and the story of Lot
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah quotes Rabbi Yochanan's parable of two people roasting a Paschal lamb, one for the mitzvah and one for gluttony. Reish Lakish objects, and they offer alternative parables involving a man with his wife and sister, and Lot and his daughters. The Gemara then discusses whether Lot intended for a mitzvah or a transgression, concluding that the entire verse was said regarding a transgression, and analyzes the verses about Lot.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah quotes Rabbi Yochanan's parable of two people roasting a Paschal lamb, one for the mitzvah and one for gluttony, applied to the verse about righteous and sinners.
Reish Lakish objects that calling the glutton a sinner is too harsh, since he still ate the Paschal lamb.
Reish Lakish offers an alternative parable of two men with their wife and sister, where one is righteous and the other a sinner.
The Gemara objects that Reish Lakish's parable involves two paths, not one path as in the verse.
The Gemara offers a parable of Lot and his two daughters, where the daughters intended for a mitzvah and Lot for a transgression.
The Gemara questions whether Lot also intended for a mitzvah.
Rabbi Yochanan states that the entire verse about Lot was said regarding a transgression.
The Gemara analyzes each phrase in the verse about Lot, linking it to other verses about sin.
The Gemara questions how Lot could be considered a sinner if he was coerced (by wine).

sub.text: Tanna quoting Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Choni
sub.text_en: Tanna quoting Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Choni
sub.desc_en: A Tanna in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Choni explains that the dot on the word 'קוּמָהּ' indicates Lot knew what happened when he arose, and he should not have drunk wine again.

items.text: Lot's separation and its consequences
items.text_en: Lot's separation and its consequences
items.desc_en: Rabba and Rava (or Rabbi Yitzchak) interpret verses about Lot: his separation from Abraham led to strife between Israel and Ammon/Moab, and his shame was revealed in synagogues and study halls through the prohibition of Ammonites and Moabites.

sub.desc_en: Rabba interprets the verse 'אח נפשע מקרית עוז ומדינים כבריח ארמון' as referring to Lot's separation from Abraham and the strife it caused between Israel and Ammon/Moab.
Rabba cites the verse 'לא יבא עמוני ומואבי בקהל ה to support that Lot's separation led to the prohibition of Ammonites and Moabites.

items.text: The value of a transgression for its own sake vs. a mitzvah not for its own sake
items.text_en: The value of a transgression for its own sake vs. a mitzvah not for its own sake
items.desc_en: Ulla compares Tamar and Zimri, noting that Tamar's sin produced kings and prophets while Zimri's caused many deaths. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that a transgression for its own sake is greater than a mitzvah not for its own sake. The Gemara questions this with Rav Yehuda's statement that one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, and reconciles by saying it is greater than a mitzvah not for its own sake. Rabbi Yochanan then discusses the seven acts of intercourse with Sisera and concludes that even the good of the wicked is bad for the righteous.

sub.desc_en: Ulla contrasts Tamar's sin, which produced kings and prophets, with Zimri's sin, which caused many Israelites to fall.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that a transgression for its own sake (לשמה) is greater than a mitzvah not for its own sake (שלא לשמה), citing the verse about Yael being more blessed than the matriarchs.
The Gemara objects by citing Rav Yehuda's statement that one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, implying its value.

The Gemara resolves that Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's statement means a transgression for its own sake is greater than a mitzvah not for its own sake (כְּמִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ), not greater than a mitzvah for its own sake.
Rabbi Yochanan states that Sisera performed seven acts of intercourse with Yael, and the Gemara questions how she could benefit from a transgression.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves that even the good of the wicked is bad for the righteous, so Yael's experience was not truly beneficial.

items.text: The reward for actions not for their own sake and the reward for a nice conversation
items.text_en: The reward for actions not for their own sake and the reward for a nice conversation
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, as the reward for Balak's forty-two sacrifices led to Ruth. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan that God does not withhold even the reward for a nice conversation, as the elder daughter's naming of Moab led to the command not to distress Moab.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, because from not-for-its-own-sake one comes to for-its-own-sake.

Rav provides evidence: as a reward for Balak's forty-two sacrifices, Ruth descended from him, as Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina states that Ruth was the granddaughter of Eglon, who was Balak's grandson.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan that God does not withhold even the reward for a nice conversation, as the elder daughter's naming of Moab led to the command not to distress Moab.

items.text: Gemara's conclusion from the earlier narrative
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion from the earlier narrative
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes from the earlier story that while the elder brother caused pain, the younger brother was not even allowed to cause pain, as per the verse 'Do not besiege them nor provoke them'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes from the earlier narrative that while the elder brother caused pain, the younger brother was not even allowed to cause pain, as per the verse 'Do not besiege them nor provoke them'.

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin's principle of precedence in mitzvot
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin's principle of precedence in mitzvot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin quotes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha that one should always precede a mitzvah, as the elder daughter (Leah) preceded the younger (Rachel) in marriage, earning the kingdom four generations earlier.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha teaches that one should always rush to perform a מצוה (commandment), as the elder sister's one-night precedence earned her four generations of kingship.

items.text: Derivation that messiah and nasi are excluded from 'me'am ha'aretz'
items.text_en: Derivation that messiah and nasi are excluded from 'me'am ha'aretz'
items.desc_en: The Tanna derives from the verse 'me'am ha'aretz' that the messiah and the nasi are excluded from the standard sin offering of a commoner. The Gemara questions this, noting that the messiah already brings a bull and the nasi a goat, but the verse is needed to teach that the messiah does not bring a lamb or goat for an unintentional sin alone.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that the verse 'מעם הארץ' excludes the anointed priest and the king from the standard sin-offering.
The Gemara objects that the messiah and king are already excluded by their distinct offerings, so why is an additional derivation needed?
The Gemara explains that the derivation is needed to teach that the messiah does not bring a ewe or goat for an unwitting action alone, but only a bull for a ruling plus action.

items.text: Question on the nasi's exclusion
items.text_en: Question on the nasi's exclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the nasi brings a goat only for an unintentional sin with a hidden matter, but for an unintentional sin alone he brings a lamb or goat, so why is the verse needed?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Granted, the anointed priest's case is understandable, but the nasi (king) brings a goat only for an unintentional sin with a hidden matter, so why is the verse needed?

items.text: Rav Zevid's first answer: case of eating chelev as a commoner and then being appointed
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's first answer: case of eating chelev as a commoner and then being appointed
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava explains the verse applies to a case where one ate an olive's bulk of chelev as a commoner, was appointed nasi, and then learned of the sin. One might think he brings a lamb or goat, so the verse teaches he brings a goat. This works for Rabbi Shimon who follows the time of knowledge, but for the Rabbis who follow the time of sin, what can be said?

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava explains the case: a commoner ate an olive's bulk of forbidden fat, was appointed prince, and then learned of his sin — one might think he brings a lamb or goat, but the verse teaches otherwise; however, this only works for Rabbi Shimon (who follows the time of awareness), not for the Rabbis (who follow the time of sin).
The Gemara objects that this works for Rabbi Shimon who follows the time of knowledge, but for the Rabbis who follow the time of sin, what can be said?

items.text: Rav Zevid's second answer: case of half an olive's bulk as a commoner and completing it as nasi
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's second answer: case of half an olive's bulk as a commoner and completing it as nasi
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava offers a different case: one ate half an olive's bulk of chelev as a commoner, was appointed nasi, and then completed the measure, and later learned. One might think the two halves combine and he brings a lamb or goat, so the verse teaches he brings a goat.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava offers a revised explanation: the case is where the commoner ate half an olive's bulk, was appointed, and then completed the measure — one might think the two halves combine for a lamb or goat, but the verse teaches otherwise.

items.text: Rava's inquiry: does the status of nasi interrupt the combination?
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry: does the status of nasi interrupt the combination?
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman: if one ate half an olive's bulk as a commoner, was appointed nasi, and then ate another half, does the nasi status prevent combination? The first half was eaten as a commoner and the second as nasi, so they do not combine, but here both halves were eaten as a commoner, so they should combine, or is there no difference?

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether the status of prince (נשיאות) interrupts the combination of two half-measures of forbidden fat eaten while a commoner, or whether they still combine.

items.text: Attempt to resolve from Ulla's statement about an apostate
items.text_en: Attempt to resolve from Ulla's statement about an apostate
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests resolving from Ulla quoting Rabbi Yochanan: if one ate chelev, set aside a sacrifice, became an apostate, and then repented, since it was rejected it remains rejected. But this is different: an apostate is not fit to bring a sacrifice, while here the person is fit.

sub.text: Gemara's attempted proof from Ulla citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Gemara's attempted proof from Ulla citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests resolving Rava's question from Ulla's statement in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that an apostate who set aside a sacrifice and then repented is rejected, but the Gemara rejects the parallel because an apostate is not fit to bring a sacrifice, whereas here the person is fit.
The Gemara rejects the proof: an apostate is not fit to bring a sacrifice, while here the person is fit.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about doubtful chevel as a commoner and then being appointed
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about doubtful chevel as a commoner and then being appointed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rav Sheshet: if one ate doubtful chelev as a commoner, was appointed nasi, and then learned of his doubt, what is the law? According to the Rabbis who follow the time of sin, he brings a suspended guilt offering. According to Rabbi Shimon, does the change in status for a definite sin also apply to a doubtful sin, or since the sacrifice (suspended guilt offering) is the same, he brings it? The Gemara concludes with 'teiku'.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rav Sheshet: if a commoner ate doubtful forbidden fat, was appointed prince, and then learned of his doubt, does the change in status affect the requirement to bring a suspensive guilt-offering (אשם תלוי)? The question is only relevant for Rabbi Shimon, not for the Rabbis.
The Gemara concludes the question with 'תיקו' (let it stand unresolved).

items.text: Derivation that a mumar is excluded from 'me'am ha'aretz'
items.text_en: Derivation that a mumar is excluded from 'me'am ha'aretz'
items.desc_en: The Tanna derives from 'me'am ha'aretz' that a mumar (apostate) is excluded from bringing a sin offering.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the phrase 'מעם הארץ' excludes an apostate (משומד) from bringing a sin-offering.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Yosei's alternative derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yosei's alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yosei in the name of Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse 'asher lo te'asenah bishgagah ve'ashem' that one who repents in his knowledge brings a sacrifice for his error, but one who does not repent does not bring a sacrifice.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Yosei citing Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yosei citing Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yosei in the name of Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse that only one who repents in his awareness brings a sacrifice for his unintentional sin, but one who does not repent does not bring a sacrifice.

items.text: Difference between the Tanna and Rabbi Shimon: a mumar for chelev who brings a sacrifice for blood
items.text_en: Difference between the Tanna and Rabbi Shimon: a mumar for chelev who brings a sacrifice for blood
items.desc_en: Rabbi Hamnuna explains the difference: a mumar for eating chelev who brings a sacrifice for blood. One holds that since he is a mumar for chelev, he is also a mumar for blood, while the other holds that regarding blood he is considered repentant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two positions (the baraita and Rabbi Shimon).

Rabbi Hamnuna explains the difference: an apostate regarding eating forbidden fat who brings a sacrifice for blood — one authority considers him an apostate for blood as well, while the other considers him repentant regarding blood.

items.text: Rava's objection and alternative explanation: eating neveilah for appetite
items.text_en: Rava's objection and alternative explanation: eating neveilah for appetite
items.desc_en: Rava objects that everyone agrees a mumar for chelev is not a mumar for blood. Rather, the dispute is about one who eats neveilah for appetite and it was replaced with forbidden fat. One holds that since he ate intentionally for appetite, he is a mumar, while the other holds that since if he had found permitted food he would not have eaten forbidden food, he is not a mumar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rava stated everyone agrees that an apostate regarding forbidden fat is not considered an apostate regarding blood.

The Gemara revises the explanation: the dispute is about a person who eats neveila (carrion) for appetite and mistakenly ate forbidden fat instead — one authority considers him an apostate, the other does not.

items.text: Definition of a mumar: eating chelev for appetite vs. to anger
items.text_en: Definition of a mumar: eating chelev for appetite vs. to anger
items.desc_en: The Tanna states: one who ate chelev is a mumar, and then asks: who is a mumar? One who eats neveilot, treifot, etc. Rabbi Yehuda adds one who wears kilayim. Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan explaining: eating chelev for appetite makes one a mumar, to anger makes one a heretic. The default mumar is one who eats neveilot, etc. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds kilayim.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states the general rule: one who ate chelev is a mumar, and then defines a mumar as one who eats neveilot, treifot, etc.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that one who wears kilayim is also a mumar.
The gemara questions the redundancy in the Tanna's statement: 'one who ate chelev is a mumar' and then 'who is a mumar? one who eats neveilot...'

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan explaining that eating chelev for appetite makes one a mumar, to anger makes one a heretic; the default mumar is one who eats neveilot, etc., and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds kilayim.

items.text: Difference between Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda and the first Tanna: rabbinic kilayim
items.text_en: Difference between Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda and the first Tanna: rabbinic kilayim
items.desc_en: The difference is regarding rabbinic kilayim: one holds that only biblical kilayim makes one a mumar, while the other holds that since the prohibition is publicized, even rabbinic kilayim makes one a mumar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two opinions regarding kilayim.

The Gemara explains: the difference is regarding rabbinic kilayim (mixed fabrics prohibited by rabbinic decree) — one authority considers it apostasy only for Torah-level kilayim, the other considers it apostasy even for rabbinic kilayim because the prohibition is well-known.
The Gemara explains that the other opinion holds that since the prohibition of kilayim is publicized, even rabbinic kilayim makes one a mumar.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina: mumar vs. heretic
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina: mumar vs. heretic
items.desc_en: Rav Acha and Ravina dispute: one says eating for appetite makes one a mumar, to anger makes one a heretic. The other says even to anger makes one a mumar, and a heretic is only an idolater. An objection is raised from a case of eating a flea or mosquito, which is to anger and is called a mumar, but that is because he says 'I will taste the taste of forbidden food'.

sub.text: Dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina
sub.text_en: Dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha and Ravina dispute: one says eating for appetite makes one an apostate, for spite a heretic; the other says even for spite one is an apostate, and a heretic is only an idolater.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that one who eats a single flea or mosquito is called an apostate, which seems to be for spite.
The Gemara resolves: there the person says 'I will taste the taste of a forbidden thing,' which is for appetite, not spite.

items.text: Definition of nasi: a king, not a tribal leader
items.text_en: Definition of nasi: a king, not a tribal leader
