items.desc_en: The Tanna teaches: who is a nasi? A king, not a tribal leader like Nachshon ben Aminadav, as the verse says 'from all the commandments of the Lord his God' and elsewhere 'to learn to fear the Lord his God'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the term 'נשיא' (prince) might include a tribal prince like Nachshon ben Aminadav, but the verse 'מכל מצות ה׳ אלהיו' (from all the commandments of the Lord his God) limits it to one who is commanded in all the commandments, like a king.

items.text: Definition of a nasi for the sin-offering
items.text_en: Definition of a nasi for the sin-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi asks Rabbi Chiya whether someone like himself (the nasi) brings a goat. Rabbi Chiya responds with a cryptic answer, and an objection is raised from a baraita about kings of Israel and Davidic kings bringing for themselves. Rabbi Chiya explains that there they are not subordinate to each other, but here they are subordinate to them. A second version of the story is given by Rav Safra, citing verses about the scepter and lawgiver.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by establishing the definition of a nasi for the sin-offering: one over whom there is only the Lord his God.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks Rabbi Chiya whether someone like himself brings a goat as a sin-offering.
Rabbi Chiya cryptically answers that Rabbi's rival in Babylonia is as great as he, implying he is not like a king.
Rabbi objects from a baraita that both kings of Israel and Davidic kings bring a goat for themselves, showing that even with a counterpart, a king brings a goat.
Rabbi Chiya resolves that there the kings were not subordinate to each other, but here the Nasi is subordinate to the Exilarch.
Rav Safra teaches a different version of the exchange.
Rabbi repeats his question about whether he brings a goat.
Rabbi Chiya answers that the Exilarch has a scepter, while the Nasi has only a ruler's staff.
A baraita is cited to support the distinction: the scepter refers to the Exilarch, and the ruler's staff to the descendants of Hillel who teach Torah.

items.text: Mishnah: Definition of mashiach and distinctions
items.text_en: Mishnah: Definition of mashiach and distinctions
items.desc_en: The mishnah defines the mashiach as the one anointed with the anointing oil, not the one with many garments. It lists the differences between the anointed high priest and the one with many garments, and between the serving high priest and the former high priest. It also lists what they have in common regarding Yom Kippur service, marriage, and mourning.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah defines the anointed priest as the one anointed with the anointing oil, not the one with many garments, and states the only difference between them is the bull brought for all commandments.
The mishnah states the only difference between a serving high priest and a former high priest is the bull of Yom Kippur and the tenth of an ephah.
The mishnah lists the commonalities between the serving and former high priests regarding Yom Kippur service, marriage, impurity, mourning, and restoring the murderer.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute about the preparation of the anointing oil
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute about the preparation of the anointing oil
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says the roots were boiled in the oil, while Rabbi Yose argues there wasn't enough oil for that, so they soaked the roots in water and floated oil on top to absorb the scent. Rabbi Yehuda responds by listing the miracles of the oil, which started as twelve log and was used for many anointings yet remains for the future.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Yehuda's position that the roots were boiled in the anointing oil.
Rabbi Yose objects that there wasn't enough oil to even coat the roots, and instead describes a method of soaking roots in water and floating oil on top to absorb the scent.

Rabbi Yehuda responds by listing multiple miracles of the oil: it started as only twelve log, yet sufficed for anointing the Tabernacle, its vessels, Aaron and his sons for seven days, and remains entirely for the future.

items.text: Another baraita: Miracles of the oil and anointing of kings
items.text_en: Another baraita: Miracles of the oil and anointing of kings
items.desc_en: Another baraita details the miracles of the anointing oil, which started as twelve log and was used for the Tabernacle, vessels, Aaron, and his sons. It states that even a high priest son of a high priest requires anointing, but a king son of a king does not, except in cases of dispute like Solomon, Joash, and Jehoahaz. The oil remains for the future, as the gematria of 'zeh' is twelve log.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse about Moses taking the anointing oil and lists the many miracles performed with the original twelve log of oil.
The baraita rules that even a high priest son of a high priest requires anointing, but a king son of a king does not.
The baraita explains that exceptions like Solomon, Joash, and Jehoahaz were anointed only because of disputes over succession.
The baraita concludes that the original oil remains for the future, as the gematria of 'זה' (this) is twelve log.

items.text: Source for anointing high priest son of high priest and king son of king
items.text_en: Source for anointing high priest son of high priest and king son of king
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'the anointed priest under him from his sons' that a high priest's son requires anointing to become high priest. For kings, Rav Acha bar Yaakov derives from the verse 'so that his days may be long in his kingdom' that it is an inheritance. Rav Pappa adds that when there is peace, the son inherits without anointing.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that even a high priest who is the son of a high priest requires anointing.
The Gemara asks for the source of this rule.
The Gemara derives from the verse 'the anointed priest under him from his sons' that only a son who is anointed becomes high priest.
Mar states that a king who is the son of a king is not anointed.
The Gemara asks for the source of this rule.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov derives from the verse 'so that his days may be long in his kingdom' that kingship is an inheritance.
The Gemara asks how we know that when there is a dispute, anointing is required.
Rav Pappa derives from the verse 'he and his sons in the midst of Israel' that when there is peace, the son inherits without anointing.

items.text: Exception for Jehu and the rule for Davidic vs. Israelite kings
items.text_en: Exception for Jehu and the rule for Davidic vs. Israelite kings
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Jehu was anointed only because of the dispute with Joram. The Gemara questions why he needed anointing since he was the first king of a new dynasty. It resolves that the baraita is incomplete and teaches that Davidic kings are anointed, but Israelite kings are not, as derived from the verse 'arise, anoint him, for this is he.' The Gemara explains that Jehu's anointing was with pure balsam oil, not the sacred oil.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that Jehu was anointed only because of the dispute with Joram.
The Gemara questions why Jehu needed anointing since he was the first king of a new dynasty.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita is incomplete and teaches that Davidic kings are anointed but Israelite kings are not.
Rava derives from the verse 'arise, anoint him, for this is he' that only this one (Davidic king) requires anointing, not others.
The Gemara objects that using sacred oil for Jehu due to Joram's dispute would be a misuse of the oil.
Rav Pappa explains that Jehu was anointed with pure balsam oil, not the sacred oil, so there was no misuse.

items.text: Clarification of Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim's ages and succession
items.text_en: Clarification of Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim's ages and succession
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the claim that Jehoiakim was two years older than Jehoahaz, citing a verse listing Josiah's sons. Rabbi Yochanan identifies Shallum as Zedekiah and Johanan as Jehoahaz. The Gemara explains that 'firstborn' refers to the first to reign, and Jehoiakim was older but not fit to succeed because he did not fill his father's place. The order of kings is clarified: Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, Zedekiah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the claim that Jehoiakim was older than Jehoahaz, citing a verse listing Josiah's sons in a different order.
Rabbi Yochanan identifies Shallum as Zedekiah and Johanan as Jehoahaz, resolving the apparent contradiction.
The Gemara explains that 'firstborn' in the verse refers to the first to reign, not the eldest by birth, so Jehoiakim was indeed older.
The Gemara questions why a younger son would reign before an older one, citing the precedent of Jehoram who reigned because he was the firstborn.
The Gemara explains that Jehoram was fit to succeed his father, whereas Jehoiakim was not, so the younger but worthy son Jehoahaz reigned first.
The Gemara questions how the same person can be both the third and fourth son in the verse's list.
The Gemara resolves that 'third' refers to birth order among sons, while 'fourth' refers to the order of kingship: Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, Zedekiah.

items.text: Why Zedekiah was called Shallum
items.text_en: Why Zedekiah was called Shallum
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that Zedekiah was called Shallum because his deeds were complete (meshullam), or because the Davidic kingdom was complete (shalma) in his days. His original name was Mattaniah, and Nebuchadnezzar renamed him Zedekiah, saying 'May God justify the judgment upon you if you rebel against me.'

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by identifying Shallum as Zedekiah and gives one reason for the name Shallum: his deeds were complete (meshullam).
An alternative explanation is given: he was called Shallum because the Davidic kingdom was complete (shalma) in his days.
The baraita clarifies that his original name was Mattaniah, citing the verse where Nebuchadnezzar renamed him Zedekiah.
Nebuchadnezzar explains the renaming: 'May God justify the judgment upon you if you rebel against me,' citing the verse about Zedekiah's rebellion.

items.text: The concealment of the anointing oil
items.text_en: The concealment of the anointing oil
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether anointing oil existed in the Second Temple era, citing a baraita that it was hidden along with the ark and other items. It explains that King Josiah hid them upon foreseeing the exile, and Rabbi Elazar derives this through verbal analogies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether anointing oil existed in the Second Temple era, citing a baraita that it was hidden along with the ark and other items.
The Gemara explains that King Josiah hid the anointing oil upon foreseeing the exile.
Rabbi Elazar derives the hiding through verbal analogies (גזירה שווה) from the words 'שם', 'משמרת', and 'דורות', and Rav Pappa clarifies that the oil was pure balsam.

items.text: The method of anointing kings and priests
items.text_en: The method of anointing kings and priests
items.desc_en: A baraita describes that kings are anointed in a crown-like shape and priests in a chi-like shape, explained as a Greek kaf. Two conflicting baraitot debate whether pouring (yetzikah) or smearing (meshichah) comes first, and the Gemara provides scriptural support for each view.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by describing the method of anointing kings and priests, with Rav Menashya bar Gadda explaining that the priest's anointing is shaped like a Greek kaf.
Two conflicting baraitot are presented: one says pouring comes first, the other says smearing comes first, and the Gemara notes that Tanna'im disagree about which is preferable.

The Gemara provides scriptural support for each view: the one who prioritizes pouring cites 'וַיִּצֹק' (he poured), while the one who prioritizes smearing argues that the pouring was only for the sake of the subsequent smearing.

items.text: The oil on Aaron's beard and the concern of me'ilah
items.text_en: The oil on Aaron's beard and the concern of me'ilah
items.desc_en: A baraita describes two drops of oil hanging from Aaron's beard like pearls. Moses worried about misuse of the oil, but a bat kol assured him there is no me'ilah. Aaron also worried, and the bat kol reassured him that neither he nor Moses misused it.

sub.desc_en: The baraita describes two drops of oil hanging from Aaron's beard like pearls, and relates Moses' concern about possible misuse of the oil, which is allayed by a bat kol.
Aaron worries that he himself might have misused the oil, but a bat kol reassures him that neither he nor Moses misused it.

items.text: Anointing kings by a spring
items.text_en: Anointing kings by a spring
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that kings are anointed only by a spring, so that their kingdom may endure, as derived from the anointing of Solomon at Gihon.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that kings are anointed only by a spring, citing Solomon's anointing at Gihon as a prooftext.

items.text: Omens and signs for success
items.text_en: Omens and signs for success
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi suggests a test using a lamp to see if one will complete the year. Other omens involve raising a chicken for business success, and seeing a shadow to know if one will return from a journey. Abaye advises eating certain foods at the start of the year as a good omen. Rav Mesharshiya gives advice to his sons about studying before their teachers and sitting by water.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi proposes a test with a lamp during the Ten Days of Repentance to determine if one will survive the year.
The gemara adds another omen: raising a chicken to test business success.
The gemara suggests a shadow test to know if one will return from a journey, but warns it is unreliable and may cause bad luck.
Abaye advises eating specific foods (gourd, fenugreek, leeks, beets, dates) at the start of the year as a good omen.

Rav Mesharshiya gives his sons advice: review the Mishnah before entering the teacher's presence, look at the teacher's mouth, study by water, and sit on the ground of Mata Mechasya rather than on the couches of Pumbedita.

items.text: Anointing with a horn vs. a flask
items.text_en: Anointing with a horn vs. a flask
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that David and Solomon, anointed with a horn, had enduring kingdoms, while Saul and Jehu, anointed with a flask, did not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that anointing with a horn (קרן) symbolizes enduring kingship, while anointing with a flask (פך) does not, citing David and Solomon as examples of the former and Saul and Jehu as examples of the latter.

items.text: The distinction between mashuach and merubeh begadim
items.text_en: The distinction between mashuach and merubeh begadim
items.desc_en: A baraita derives that the 'mashiach' in the verse refers specifically to the anointed priest, not a king or a war anointed. Rava explains the derivation. The Gemara clarifies that the mishnah excludes Rabbi Meir, who holds that a merubeh begadim also brings a bull for all commandments, while the Sages disagree.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse and derives that 'mashiach' refers specifically to the anointed priest, excluding a king, a מרובה בגדים (priest with many garments), and a war-anointed priest.
Rava explains the derivation by analogy to 'the thigh' meaning the chosen one of the thigh, so 'the mashiach' means the chosen one among the anointed.

The Gemara objects that a king brings a goat, not a bull, so why would one think he brings a bull? It answers that one might have thought a king brings a goat for an action and a bull for a hidden matter, so the verse teaches otherwise.
The Gemara concludes that the mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Meir, who holds that a מרובה בגדים (priest with many garments) also brings a bull for all commandments, while the Sages disagree.
The Gemara cites a baraita that gives Rabbi Meir's reasoning: from 'mashiach' one only knows the anointed priest, but a מרובה בגדים (priest with many garments) is derived from 'the anointed priest'.
The Gemara concludes that the mishnah is established in accordance with the Sages, who reject Rabbi Meir's view.

items.text: The case of a disqualified High Priest and his replacement
items.text_en: The case of a disqualified High Priest and his replacement
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a baraita about a High Priest who was disqualified and replaced, citing the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei regarding the status of the replacement. Rabbi Yosei brings a story about Yosef ben Ila'im to support his position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the end of the Mishnah and identifies it as following Rabbi Meir's position.
A baraita is cited presenting the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei regarding the status of a replaced High Priest.
Rabbi Yosei brings a story about Yosef ben Ila'im to support his position that the replacement cannot serve even as an ordinary priest.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the beginning and end of the Mishnah, and offers three resolutions: Rav Chisda attributes the beginning to the Rabbis and the end to Rabbi Meir; Rav Yosef says it is Rabbi's version aligned with the Tannaim; Rava says it is Rabbi Shimon who agrees with Rabbi Meir on one point and disagrees on another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can attribute the beginning to the Rabbis and the end to Rabbi Meir.
Rav Chisda affirms that the beginning reflects the Rabbis and the end reflects Rabbi Meir.
Rav Yosef says the Mishnah is Rabbi's version, aligned with the Tannaim.
Rava says the Mishnah is Rabbi Shimon's, who agrees with Rabbi Meir on one point and disagrees on another.

items.text: The list of differences between High Priest and ordinary priest
items.text_en: The list of differences between High Priest and ordinary priest
items.desc_en: A baraita enumerates the differences between a High Priest and an ordinary priest, including the bull for all commandments, the bull of Yom Kippur, the tenth of an ephah, and various prohibitions. It also discusses which laws apply to a priest who served in eight garments, a former High Priest, and a priest anointed for war.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists the differences between a High Priest and an ordinary priest, including Rabbi Yehuda's and the Sages' opinions on returning the murderer.

The baraita continues listing additional differences: the High Priest offers while an onen (mourner before burial) but does not eat, serves in eight garments, and is exempt from the penalty for טומאת מקדש וקדשיו (impurity of the Temple and its holy things).

The baraita concludes by specifying which laws apply to a priest who served in eight garments (מרובה בגדים), a former High Priest (משיח שעבר), and a priest anointed for war (משוח מלחמה), with a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding the latter's power to return a murderer.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the baraita as Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the baraita as Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa identifies the baraita as Rabbi Shimon's because it includes the exemption for impurity of the Temple and its holy things, which is a view unique to Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the baraita is Rabbi Shimon's.
Rav Pappa identifies Rabbi Shimon as the one who says a High Priest is exempt from the sin-offering for טומאת מקדש וקדשיו (impurity of the Temple and its holy things).

items.text: Derivation of the five special laws for the anointed for war
items.text_en: Derivation of the five special laws for the anointed for war
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the five laws that apply to the priest anointed for war from the verse 'The great priest from among his brothers', interpreting the terms to include the High Priest, the anointed for war, and the priest who served in many garments. It then discusses the derivation of the prohibition against marrying a widow and the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva regarding a priest who was disqualified due to a blemish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these five matters derived?

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the five laws from the verse 'והכהן הגדול מאחיו' (the great priest from among his brothers), interpreting the terms to include the High Priest, the anointed for war, and the priest who served in many garments.
The Gemara asks: One might have thought that all these priests sacrifice offerings as acute mourners.

The Gemara answers: The verse states 'כי נזר שמן משחת אלהיו עליו' (for the consecration of the anointing oil of his God is upon him), teaching that this applies only to him and not to another; and after the verse differentiated, it includes the anointed for war with the word 'והוא' (and he).

The Gemara notes a dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva: Rabbi Yishmael holds that after the verse distinguished, it included the anointed for war; Rabbi Akiva holds that the verse 'והוא' includes only a High Priest who stepped down due to blemishes.

items.text: The case of a leprous High Priest and the widow
items.text_en: The case of a leprous High Priest and the widow
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether a High Priest who became a leper is prohibited from marrying a widow or exempt from the prohibition. The question is unresolved until Huna, Rav Nachman's son, cites a baraita that includes a priest disqualified due to a blemish, which implies that a leprous priest is also prohibited. Rav Pappa then kisses him and gives him his daughter.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether a High Priest who became a leper is temporarily disqualified from service (and thus still prohibited from marrying a widow) or totally absolved of his status (and thus permitted). Rav Nachman has no answer.

Huna bar Rav Nachman cites a baraita that includes a priest disqualified due to blemishes (including leprosy) in the prohibition against marrying a widow, resolving the question. Rav Pappa kisses him and gives him his daughter in appreciation.

items.text: The Mishnah on rending garments and the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: The Mishnah on rending garments and the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a High Priest rends his garment from below, while an ordinary priest rends from above. The Gemara brings a dispute between Rav and Shmuel about the meaning of 'below' and 'above'. A challenge is raised from a baraita, and Shmuel is reconciled with Rabbi Yehuda's view, though a contradiction is noted from another baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says a High Priest does not rend at all. The Gemara concludes that Shmuel agrees with Rabbi Yehuda on one point and disagrees on another.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a High Priest rends his garment from below and an ordinary priest from above, and that a High Priest may offer sacrifices while an onen (mourner) but not eat, while an ordinary priest may neither offer nor eat.

The Gemara brings a dispute between Rav and Shmuel: Rav says 'below' means literally below the neck, and 'above' means literally above; Shmuel says 'below' means below the hem of the collar, and 'above' means above the hem, but both rend in the neck area.

A challenge is raised from a baraita: for all deceased, one may choose to rend above or below the collar hem, but for a parent one must rend above the hem; this implies that a High Priest, who is prohibited from rending, would violate the verse 'his garments he shall not rend' if he rends at all.

The Gemara explains that Shmuel holds like Rabbi Yehuda, who says that any rending that does not separate the hem is a worthless tear, so Shmuel's interpretation of 'below' and 'above' refers to the hem, not the neck.
The Gemara objects: does Rabbi Yehuda actually allow any rending for a High Priest?
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda says the verse teaches that a High Priest has no obligation to rend at all, while Rabbi Yishmael says he rends from below and an ordinary priest from above.

The Gemara concludes that Shmuel agrees with Rabbi Yehuda on one point (that rending must separate the hem) but disagrees on another (that a High Priest does rend, unlike Rabbi Yehuda's absolute exemption).

items.text: The principle of precedence: frequent and sanctified
items.text_en: The principle of precedence: frequent and sanctified
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a more frequent offering precedes a less frequent one, and a more sanctified offering precedes a less sanctified one. The Gemara derives the principle of frequency from the verse 'besides the burnt offering of the morning, which is for the continual burnt offering', and the principle of sanctity from the verse 'and you shall sanctify him' for all matters of sanctity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the principle that a more frequent offering precedes a less frequent one, and a more sanctified offering precedes a less sanctified one, with the example of the anointed priest's bull preceding the congregation's bull.
The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (the principle of frequency) derived?

Abaye answers by citing the verse 'besides the burnt offering of the morning, which is for the continual burnt offering', explaining that the extra phrase teaches that anything more frequent takes precedence.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the principle that a more sanctified offering precedes a less sanctified one?

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael answers by citing the verse 'וְקִדַּשְׁתּוֹ' (and you shall sanctify him), which teaches that the more sanctified person takes precedence in all matters of sanctity: to open first, to bless first, and to take a good portion first.

items.text: Precedence of the anointed priest's bull over the congregation's bull
items.text_en: Precedence of the anointed priest's bull over the congregation's bull
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a verse that the bull of the anointed priest precedes the bull of the congregation in all its actions, and a baraita explains the logic: the one who atones precedes the one being atoned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's ruling that the anointed priest's bull precedes the congregation's bull.

A baraita cites the verse 'וְשָׂרַף אוֹתוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁר שָׂרַף אֵת הַפָּר הָרִאשׁוֹן' to derive that the anointed priest's bull is called 'first' and thus precedes the congregation's bull in all its actions.

Another baraita explicitly states that the anointed priest's bull precedes the congregation's bull in all actions, because the one who atones (המכפר) precedes the one being atoned (המתכפר), as the verse says 'וְכִפֶּר בַּעֲדוֹ וּבְעַד בֵּיתוֹ וּבְעַד כׇּל קְהַל יִשְׂרָאֵל'.

items.text: Precedence of the bull for unwitting sin over the bull for idolatry
items.text_en: Precedence of the bull for unwitting sin over the bull for idolatry
items.desc_en: The bull for an unwitting communal sin (a sin-offering) precedes the bull for idolatry (a burnt-offering), based on the principle that sin-offerings always precede burnt-offerings that accompany them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the bull for an unwitting communal sin precedes the bull for idolatry.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind this precedence.

The Gemara explains that the bull for unwitting sin is a sin-offering (חטאת) and the bull for idolatry is a burnt-offering (עולה), and a baraita establishes that all sin-offerings precede accompanying burnt-offerings, even a bird sin-offering before a beast burnt-offering.

items.text: Precedence of the bull for idolatry over the goat for idolatry
items.text_en: Precedence of the bull for idolatry over the goat for idolatry
items.desc_en: The bull for idolatry (a sin-offering) precedes the goat for idolatry (a burnt-offering). Two explanations are given: one based on a missing letter in the verse, and another based on the word 'as per the ordinance' written regarding it.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks why the bull for idolatry (a sin-offering) precedes the goat for idolatry (a burnt-offering), given the general rule that sin-offerings precede burnt-offerings.

sub.text: Rava bar Mari's answer (from the West)
sub.text_en: Rava bar Mari's answer (from the West)
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Mari answers that the bull for idolatry is missing the letter 'alef' in its verse (written 'לחטאת' instead of 'לחטאת'), indicating a special status.
Rava answers that the verse writes 'as per the ordinance' (כמשפט) regarding the bull, giving it precedence.

items.text: Precedence among goats and sheep for individuals
items.text_en: Precedence among goats and sheep for individuals
items.desc_en: The goat for idolatry precedes the goat for a prince (communal vs. individual), the prince's goat precedes an individual's goat (king vs. commoner), and a dispute arises whether an individual's goat precedes an individual's lamb or vice versa, resolved by Abaye as a tannaitic dispute.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the precedence: the goat for idolatry precedes the prince's goat, and the prince's goat precedes an individual's she-goat.
The gemara questions the mishnah's ruling that an individual's she-goat precedes his lamb, citing a baraita that reverses the order.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by attributing the dispute to a tannaitic disagreement: one Tanna holds the she-goat is superior because it is brought for idolatry by an individual.
The other Tanna holds the lamb is superior because it is brought with its fat tail (אליה), which is offered on the altar.

items.text: Precedence of the omer and two loaves over accompanying lambs
items.text_en: Precedence of the omer and two loaves over accompanying lambs
items.desc_en: The omer precedes the lamb that comes with it, and the two loaves precede the lambs that come with them, based on the rule: something that comes for the day precedes something that comes for the bread.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the omer precedes its accompanying lamb, and the two loaves precede their accompanying lambs, with the general rule that something coming for the day precedes something coming for the bread.

items.text: Precedence for saving life and redeeming captives
items.text_en: Precedence for saving life and redeeming captives
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man precedes a woman for saving life and returning lost property, but a woman precedes a man for clothing and redemption from captivity. The Gemara adds that if a person, his father, and his teacher are in captivity, he precedes his teacher, and his teacher precedes his father; his mother precedes all.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule that a man precedes a woman for saving life and returning lost property, but a woman precedes a man for clothing and redemption from captivity, and when both are in equal danger, the man precedes.
The Gemara cites a baraita that elaborates on the order of precedence for redemption from captivity: a person precedes his teacher, his teacher precedes his father, and his mother precedes all.

items.text: Precedence among sages, kings, high priests, and prophets
items.text_en: Precedence among sages, kings, high priests, and prophets
items.desc_en: A sage precedes a king of Israel, a king precedes a high priest, and a high priest precedes a prophet, each supported by biblical verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a sage precedes a king of Israel, because a sage has no replacement while any Israelite is fit for kingship.
The Gemara proves that a king precedes a high priest from the verse where King Solomon commands to take the servants of Adoniyahu.

The Gemara proves that a high priest precedes a prophet from the verse where Zadok the priest is mentioned before Nathan the prophet, and from the verse calling Joshua the high priest and his colleagues 'men of wonder' (prophets).

items.text: Precedence among various priestly roles
items.text_en: Precedence among various priestly roles
items.desc_en: A hierarchy is established: anointed with anointing oil precedes one with many garments, who precedes a past anointed due to exile, who precedes one with a blemish, who precedes the priest anointed for war, who precedes the deputy, who precedes the amarkal, who precedes the treasurer, who precedes the head of the watch, who precedes the head of the paternal house, who precedes a common priest.

sub.desc_en: Establishes the hierarchy of priestly roles from the anointed high priest down to the war priest.
Rav Chisda defines 'amarkal' as 'amar kolla' (says everything) and completes the hierarchy down to the common priest.

items.text: Dispute: deputy vs. anointed for war regarding impurity
items.text_en: Dispute: deputy vs. anointed for war regarding impurity
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised about which of the deputy or the anointed for war takes precedence regarding impurity. A baraita indicates the anointed for war should become impure rather than the deputy, but another baraita says the anointed for war precedes the deputy. Ravina resolves that the latter refers to saving life.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: regarding impurity, which of the deputy (סגן) or the anointed for war (משוח מלחמה) takes precedence?

Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman cites a baraita: if the deputy and the anointed for war encounter a met mitzvah (unattended corpse), it is better that the anointed for war become impure rather than the deputy, because the deputy may need to serve in place of the High Priest.
The Gemara objects: but another baraita explicitly states that the anointed for war precedes the deputy.
Ravina resolves: that baraita refers to saving the deputy's life (להחיותו), where the anointed for war takes precedence.

items.text: Precedence among Jewish lineages
items.text_en: Precedence among Jewish lineages
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the order: priest, Levite, Israelite, mamzer, netin, convert, freed slave. The Gemara provides reasons for each, based on lineage, holiness, and curses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the order of precedence among Jewish lineages: priest, Levite, Israelite, mamzer, netin, convert, freed slave.
The Mishnah qualifies that this order applies only when all are equal in Torah knowledge; a mamzer who is a Torah scholar precedes an ignorant high priest.
The Gemara provides scriptural proof for the priest preceding the Levite (from Chronicles) and the Levite preceding the Israelite (from Deuteronomy).

The Gemara explains each step: Israelite over mamzer due to lineage, mamzer over netin due to fit seed, netin over convert due to growing up in holiness, convert over freed slave due to being under the curse of Ham.

items.text: Exception: Torah scholar precedes ignorant high priest
items.text_en: Exception: Torah scholar precedes ignorant high priest
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's rule applies only when all are equal; but a mamzer who is a Torah scholar precedes a high priest who is an ignoramus, derived from the verse 'It is more precious than pearls' (referring to Torah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's exception.

Rav Acha bar Rabbi Chanina derives the rule from the verse 'יְקָרָה הִיא מִפְּנִינִים' (it is more precious than pearls), meaning a Torah scholar precedes even a high priest who enters the Holy of Holies.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's alternative view on freed slave vs. convert
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's alternative view on freed slave vs. convert
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai argues that a freed slave should precede a convert because he grew up in holiness, but the Gemara notes that the convert was not under the curse, so the Mishnah's order stands.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai argues that a freed slave should precede a convert because he grew up in holiness.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's order stands because the convert was under the curse of Adam, while the freed slave was not.

items.text: Questions about converts, freed slaves, and animals
items.text_en: Questions about converts, freed slaves, and animals
items.desc_en: Students ask Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok why people prefer to marry a female convert over a freed slave, and why a dog recognizes its owner but a cat does not. They also ask Rabbi Eliezer why mice are dominated; answers involve curses and nature.

sub.text: Students' question to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok
sub.text_en: Students' question to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok
sub.desc_en: Students ask Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok why everyone runs to marry a female convert but not a freed slave woman.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok answers that the freed slave woman was under the curse of Canaan, and additionally she was not presumed to be guarded from sexual immorality.
Students ask Rabbi Elazar why a dog recognizes its owner but a cat does not.
Rabbi Elazar answers that since a cat eats mice, which are forgetful creatures, it inherits forgetfulness, while a dog does not eat mice.
Students ask Rabbi Eliezer why everyone dominates mice, and he answers because their nature is bad.
Rava explains the bad nature of mice: they even gnaw through cloaks.

items.text: Rav Pappa's opening statement
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's opening statement
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says that even a shared axe handle becomes worn out (i.e., constant use wears things out, perhaps introducing the theme of factors affecting study).

items.text: Baraita: Five things that cause forgetfulness and five that restore
items.text_en: Baraita: Five things that cause forgetfulness and five that restore
items.desc_en: A baraita lists five things that cause a person to forget their learning, and five things that restore it, with an additional opinion for each list.

items.text: Gemara supports for olive oil and wine/spices
items.text_en: Gemara supports for olive oil and wine/spices
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan that olives cause forgetfulness of seventy years of study, while olive oil restores it, supporting the baraita. It also cites Rava that wine and spices make one sharp, supporting the baraita's inclusion of wine and spices.

items.text: Resh Lakish and the dispute about dipping a finger in salt
items.text_en: Resh Lakish and the dispute about dipping a finger in salt
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish qualifies the practice of dipping a finger in salt, saying it is only effective with one finger. This is supported by a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda (one, not two) and Rabbi Yosei (two, not three), with a mnemonic of 'kemitzah'.

items.text: Baraita: Ten things that are hard for study
items.text_en: Baraita: Ten things that are hard for study
items.desc_en: A baraita lists ten things that are difficult for Torah study, including passing under a camel's halter, between two women, eating undercooked bread, and looking at a dead person's face, with an additional opinion about reading writing on a grave.

items.text: Baraita: Protocol for entering the study hall based on rank
items.text_en: Baraita: Protocol for entering the study hall based on rank
items.desc_en: A baraita details the protocol for entering the study hall: for the Nasi, everyone stands and sits only when told; for the Av Beit Din, two rows are formed; for a Sage, one stands and one sits; for sons of Sages, they step over people's heads if needed; and if one leaves for a need, they return and sit in their place.

items.text: Baraita: Sons of Torah scholars who are appointed as leaders
items.text_en: Baraita: Sons of Torah scholars who are appointed as leaders
items.desc_en: The baraita continues: sons of Torah scholars whose father is a communal leader sit before their father, with their backs to the people if they are mature enough to listen, and facing the people if not. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok adds that even at a wedding feast they are made into supports.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rava on leaving for a need
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rava on leaving for a need
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa qualifies the rule about leaving for a need: it applies only to small needs, but for large needs one should have checked themselves beforehand, citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav. Rava adds that nowadays, due to weakness, even for large needs it applies.

items.text: Rava qualifies Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's statement
items.text_en: Rava qualifies Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's statement
items.desc_en: Rava qualifies Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's statement about making sons supports at a wedding feast: it applies only during their father's lifetime and in their father's presence.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan: The mishnah was taught in the days of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan: The mishnah was taught in the days of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that this mishnah (about protocol) was taught in the days of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, when he was Nasi, Rabbi Meir was Sage, and Rabbi Natan was Av Beit Din. Everyone stood for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and also for Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Natan, so Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel instituted this mishnah to create a distinction.

items.text: The next day: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Natan are not honored
items.text_en: The next day: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Natan are not honored
items.desc_en: The next day, when Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Natan came, they saw that people did not stand for them as before. They asked why, and were told that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel had instituted this protocol.

items.text: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Natan plot to depose Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Natan plot to depose Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir proposes to Rabbi Natan that they devise a plan to embarrass Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel by asking him to teach tractate Uktzin, which he hasn't studied, and then depose him, making Rabbi Natan Nasi and Rabbi Meir Av Beit Din.

items.text: Rabbi Yaakov ben Kudshai overhears and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel prepares
items.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov ben Kudshai overhears and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel prepares
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov ben Kudshai overhears the plot and, fearing embarrassment, goes behind Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's attic, reviews tractate Uktzin repeatedly. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel hears, suspects something, and also reviews it. The next day, when asked to teach Uktzin, he does so successfully and then rebukes them.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel expels Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Natan
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel expels Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Natan
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel orders Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Natan expelled from the study hall. They write questions on notes and throw them in, and answers are written back. Rabbi Yosei protests that Torah is outside while they are inside.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allows them back but penalizes them
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allows them back but penalizes them
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel agrees to let them back but penalizes them so that their teachings are not cited in their names. Rabbi Meir is called 'Acherim' and Rabbi Natan 'Yesh Omrim'. They are told in a dream to appease him. Rabbi Natan goes, but Rabbi Meir does not, saying dreams are meaningless. Rabbi Natan is rebuked by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

items.text: Rabbi teaches his son: Acherim say about temurah
items.text_en: Rabbi teaches his son: Acherim say about temurah
items.desc_en: Rabbi teaches his son Rabban Shimon that 'Acherim say: If it were a temurah...'

items.text: The anonymous citation and the identity of the sage
items.text_en: The anonymous citation and the identity of the sage
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions who is the sage whose water they drink but whose name they do not mention. It is revealed that he sought to uproot the honor of the Nasi and his father's house. The Gemara then discusses the verse about love and hate being lost, and concludes that this applies only when their deeds were effective, but the Rabbis' deeds were not. The teaching is then cited in the name of Rabbi Meir, and Rava notes that even the humble Rabbi (the Nasi) used the phrase 'they said in the name of Rabbi Meir' rather than 'Rabbi Meir said'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the anonymous sage whose water they drink but whose name they do not mention.
The sage answers that they are people who sought to uproot the honor of the Nasi and his father's house.
The Nasi objects by citing the verse that their love, hate, and envy have already perished.
The sage responds with another verse that the enemy's destructions are finished forever.
The Nasi resolves that the verse applies only when their deeds were effective, but the Rabbis' deeds were not.
The teaching is then cited in the name of Rabbi Meir: if it were a substitute, it would not be offered.
Rava notes that even the humble Rabbi (the Nasi) used the phrase 'they said in the name of Rabbi Meir' rather than 'Rabbi Meir said'.

items.text: The dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis: Sinai vs. Oker Harim
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis: Sinai vs. Oker Harim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis disagree: one says a 'Sinai' (one with broad knowledge) is superior, and the other says an 'Oker Harim' (one who uproots mountains through sharp argumentation) is superior.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports a dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis: one holds that a 'Sinai' (broad knowledge) is superior, the other that an 'Oker Harim' (sharp dialectician) is superior.

items.text: The application to Rav Yosef and Rabbah, and the practical outcome
items.text_en: The application to Rav Yosef and Rabbah, and the practical outcome
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef is identified as a 'Sinai' and Rabbah as an 'Oker Harim'. They sent to Eretz Yisrael to ask which is given precedence, and the reply was that the 'Sinai' is superior, citing the principle that all need the master of wheat. Nevertheless, Rav Yosef did not accept the position. Rabbah ruled for 22 years, and then Rav Yosef ruled. During Rabbah's reign, Rav Yosef did not even serve as a craftsman in his house.

sub.desc_en: The gemara identifies Rav Yosef as a 'Sinai' (master of broad knowledge) and Rabbah as an 'Oker Harim' (master of sharp dialectics).
They sent to Eretz Yisrael to ask which of the two is given precedence.
The reply was that the 'Sinai' is superior, citing the principle that all need the master of wheat.
Nevertheless, Rav Yosef did not accept the position; Rabbah ruled for 22 years, then Rav Yosef ruled, and during Rabbah's reign Rav Yosef did not even serve as a craftsman in his house.

items.text: The appointment of Abaye as head
items.text_en: The appointment of Abaye as head
items.desc_en: Abaye, Rava, Rabbi Zeira, and Rabbah bar Mattana were sitting and needed a head. They agreed that whoever says a statement that is not refuted should be head. All were refuted except Abaye. Rabbah saw that Abaye was becoming haughty and told him to open and speak.

sub.desc_en: The gemara sets the scene: Abaye, Rava, Rabbi Zeira, and Rabbah bar Mattana were sitting and needed a head, so they agreed that whoever says a statement that is not refuted should be head.
All were refuted except Abaye; Rabbah saw that Abaye was becoming haughty and told him to open and speak.

items.text: The unresolved question between Rabbi Zeira and Rabbah bar Rav Mattana
items.text_en: The unresolved question between Rabbi Zeira and Rabbah bar Rav Mattana
items.desc_en: A question was raised: between Rabbi Zeira and Rabbah bar Rav Mattana, which is superior? Rabbi Zeira is sharp and raises difficulties, while Rabbah bar Rav Mattana is deliberate and reaches conclusions. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises an unresolved question (תיקו) about which sage is superior: Rabbi Zeira, who is sharp and raises difficulties, or Rabbah bar Rav Mattana, who is deliberate and reaches conclusions.
